<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README details, this project is clearly an implementation of an OCI Container Runtime written completely in C, with a focus on low memory overhead and high performance. It is not just a command‐line tool but also exposes a library (libcrun) that can be embedded in other applications. The project also includes support for Lua bindings and optional Python integrations for OCI specifications. Here’s how you can approach creating a detailed system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   - CLI & Orchestration Layer: Files like src/crun.c, src/create.c, src/start.c, src/exec.c, etc., form the command-line interface and process control layer for container operations.
   - Core Container Runtime Library (libcrun): The most significant part is found under src/libcrun. This submodule includes modules for container lifecycle management, cgroup support, seccomp filtering, signal handling, mount management, and even specialized handlers for various container backends (like Mono, WASM runtimes, etc. in handlers/).
   - OS Integration & System Interfaces: There is heavy interaction with Linux kernel features such as cgroups (files like cgroup-cgroupfs.c, cgroup-systemd.c, and related utilities), seccomp (seccomp.c, seccomp_notify.c), and namespace handling. This represents the interface that crun uses to create, monitor, and clean-up container processes.
   - Build and Configuration Infrastructure: Scripts like autogen.sh, configure.ac, Makefile.am, cfg.mk, and directories like build-aux and m4 denote a conventional GNU autotools build system – highlighting configurable and modular build aspects.
   - Contributed Plugins and Examples: Look at the contrib/ directory (e.g., seccomp-notify-plugin-example, terminal-receiver, etc.) which offer extensibility points and integration examples for notification and seccomp handling.
   - Bindings / Language Integrations: The lua/ directory (including lua_crun.c and related rockspec files) shows that there is a Lua binding available, while the python/ directory supports Python integrations (evidenced by crun_python.c).
   - Tests & Validation: The tests/ directory includes various Dockerfiles, shell scripts, and unit tests (including tests for capabilities, seccomp, mounts, etc.) to ensure system compliance with OCI specs and robust functionality.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   - The CLI layer interacts with the core libcrun library to perform operations such as container creation, delete, exec, and update. These operations are all defined in corresponding source files (e.g., create.c, exec.c, etc.).
   - libcrun then interacts directly with the Linux kernel interfaces (via cgroups, seccomp, namespaces, etc.) to enforce isolation, resource limits, and security policies.
   - The plugin handlers (e.g., from handlers/ directory) allow for integration with additional functionalities like support for various container runtimes or extensions for languages (e.g., WASM runtimes).
   - The build configuration and scripts manage how the overall project pieces are combined, enabling static and shared builds, and even integration with reproducible package systems like Nix.
   - The tests simulate different runtime scenarios, ensuring that each component (from CLI processing to OS API interactions) meets the defined OCI specifications.

3. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   - Modularization: There is a clear separation between the command interface and the core runtime library.
   - Layered Design: Higher-level commands (CLI layer) call into lower-level, specialized modules (libcrun) that directly communicate with the OS.
   - Extensibility: The presence of a plugins directory and bindings for multiple programming languages indicates an architectural intention to allow for future enhancements or integrations.
   - Isolation and Abstraction: The runtime cleanly abstracts away complex interactions with kernel level features (cgroups, seccomp) from the user-facing operations.

4. Diagram Guidelines & Inclusions:
   - Represent each major component as a distinct box or module:
     • CLI & Command Manager (container create, run, exec, kill, etc.)
     • Core Runtime Library – libcrun (subdivide as needed into container lifecycle, cgroup management, seccomp filtering, etc.)
     • OS/Kernel Interfaces (cgroups, seccomp, namespaces, system calls)
     • Extensibility/Plugin Modules (seccomp notify plugins, terminal receiver, etc.)
     • Bindings/Integrations (Lua, Python)
     • Build & Deployment Infrastructure (autotools scripts, Nix, RPM packaging)
     • Testing Framework (various Dockerfiles and test scripts)
   - Use directional arrows to show how data flows and control moves:
     • From the CLI components into the libcrun core.
     • From libcrun to the OS for system-level operations.
     • From test modules towards the core logic to simulate real container operations.
   - Clearly label each component with its purpose and technology (e.g., “libcrun: Container Lifecycle & Resource Isolation”, “CLI: User Command Processor”).
   - You may consider color coding components to differentiate between user-space layers (CLI, libcrun) and underlying system interfaces (kernel and OS features). Shapes can also be used to distinguish between static libraries, dynamic libraries, and external integrations.
   - Highlight the configurable nature of the build (shown by the presence of build scripts, autotools, and Nix derivations) which might influence how the system is deployed.

5. Tailoring to the Specific Project:
   - For this full-stack container runtime tool, make sure your diagram emphasizes the clear separation between:
     • The control logic (CLI and command handlers) that processes user inputs and orchestrates container lifecycle events.
     • The core execution module (libcrun) that carries out actual container management using well-established Linux kernel features.
     • External testing and build/deployment systems ensuring portability and reliability.
   - Include relevant technologies and dependencies (for example, libseccomp, systemd integration, Linux cgroup frameworks) that are specified in the README and the file tree.
  
Remember: While drawing the system design diagram, it’s best to decompose the project into as many meaningful components as possible. Being detailed ensures that every critical architectural element—from the external interfaces to the in-house libraries—is clearly annotated and connected with dependency arrows. This high level of detail will aid in understanding the overall system flow and pinpointing areas for future improvements or troubleshooting.

Use these instructions to create a comprehensive yet clearly segmented diagram that maps all aspects of crun’s architecture and its interactions with both internal modules and external operating system services.
</explanation>
